newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Watershed for telecoms industry as prices fall.
newsitem.headline: Watershed for telecoms industry as prices fall.

text.p: The world's telecommunications industry is booming as microchip technology offers increasingly sophisticated services to ever more remote parts of the globe.

Asia's largest telecom fair in Singapore last week bristled with all the latest gizmos offered by thousands of companies -- mobile phones and pagers, interactive information, video and music and satellite communication devices.

But the traditional structure of the industry, which will see revenues of around US$1 trillion this year, is under increasing pressure from new technology that is driving down costs and allowing new players to emerge.
The explosion of computer capacity has produced tiny computer chips that are so fast, powerful and cheap that the cost of making a phone call has collapsed.
This is speeding up the liberalisation of national and international regulations and shattering the status quo.
The giant telephone companies, which once enjoyed unrivalled profits, are being forced to cut prices to stay in business.
"Monopoly profits and excessive returns are disappearing fast and the companies have to adapt," said Gautam Kapoor, regional telecommunications analyst for ING Baring.

The traditionally conservative industry regulator, the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), recognises that the high profits enjoyed by telecom companies are a thing of the past and need to fall if the industry is to develop.
"Even the lowest rates in the world today are too high. They are well above real costs," ITU Secretary-General Pekka Tarjanne told Reuters.
New telecom entrants are more scathing.
Colin Williams, head of U.S. telecoms group WorldCom Inc, part of a consortium seeking a Singapore telephone system licence, called international phone call profits obscene.
"The telecoms companies will have to start providing services at prices which give them a reasonable return but not the obscene returns which the industry has required," he said.
Over the next five years, the cost of transmitting data long-distance may well fall by 90 percent, and voice costs almost as much, he said.
The computer revolution is changing the nature of the industry from one providing voice transmission to one based mainly on sophisticated data.
Analysts expect the current 80-20 ratio of voice to data will be reversed with five years.
The data explosion is driven by the computerisation of commerce and the Internet, which threatens to absorb the traditional market for telephone calls.
Although voice quality is still poor, Internet phoning is so quick and cheap that many experts think it may soon become the main means of international communication.
Bill Gates, who has cornered the world's software market through his company Microsoft, believes telecoms firms must embrace the Internet or will lose out.
"I expect Internet telephony to increase," he told the conference. The cost of making a call on the Internet is less than a 10th of the cost of a traditional phone call, he said.
Because Internet telephony allows users to pay local rates for a long-distance call, it is helping undermine the traditional system of charging for international telephony.
Analysts say the Internet could destroy the much criticised "accounting rate" system used to work out how international calls are priced.

Tarjanne argues that technology and competition have made the accounting rate system -- developed when international calls were made between giant monopolies -- obsolete, and says it should be scrapped in favour of a cost-based system.
There are bound to be many casualties in the industry over the next few years.
Williams argues the survivors will be those that can cope with the changes and offer special services:
"In the future there will be a small number of very large players and an awful lot of niche players. But who will be the winners and the losers is all part of the fun of the game."
